title: Mòr nic Dhùghaill feeds three carriers in the rain
summary: A widow of Doire shean with more buffalo than grass boils a haunch for three carriers caught by a mud-slicked path, and asks no coin for it. Word of the free bowl travels the mountain road faster than any basket on it, and within a year she has built a second room to feed the men it sends her.

title: The turf longhouse raised at the crossing
summary: Three families of the fourth hearth build a long turf house where the mountain road meets the road to the western harbours, a hearth burning at either end for carriers going up and carriers coming down. Its long central table becomes the place where news of the whole road first gathers as one telling.

title: A chase stopped at Mòr's door
summary: A man fleeing his cousin's kin over an old knife-wound takes shelter at Mòr nic Dhùghaill's table, and his three pursuers, knives at their belts, find her standing between them and the fire. She swears there will be no blade drawn under her roof for any grievance, old or new, and feeds all four from the one pot until the debt walks back out onto the open road unsettled between them.

title: The road-peace kept as custom
summary: Word of the chase stopped at Mòr's door runs the mountain road faster than any basket that season, and other waypoint houses along the circuit take up the same custom unasked: no feud pursued and no blade drawn under a road-house roof or within a spear's throw of its door.

title: Niall Òg sits at Mòr's table
summary: The old heir Niall Òg walks the mountain road to see for himself the house where a widow's word held two feuding kin to one table, and is given the same bowl and the same seat as any other traveller. He leaves a ring behind that Mòr will not keep, saying a man who has outlived his own quarrels can afford, once in a while, to pay for a peace he did not make.

title: Seann Mhorn resettled and its name kept
summary: Fishers of the nine hearths find old house-footings above a good landing on the western shore of Loch chrom, and a name already fixed to the place that is not of their own tongue. They keep the name rather than giving it a new one, judging that a name found standing has more right to stay than one a stranger could invent.

title: Seann Warr resettled beside it
summary: Families walking the same road find a second harbour a short way along the shore, house-footings there as well, and build on them without asking whose. Seann Warr and Seann Mhorn grow together within the century, sharing a landing, a market day and a single waypoint house where the mountain road meets the sea.

title: Fionnlagh Dall asks to be carried south
summary: Dying at four-and-ninety after fifty-six years keeping the flame, Fionnlagh Dall tells Calum Beag he wishes to be laid not on the Keepers' own slope but in the unclaimed old graves near Cnoc dhìreach, ground no household's cord has ever divided. He dies within the month, his last words a question about whether the flame had been fed.

title: The eleven days' bearing
summary: Bearers carry Fionnlagh Dall's body the twenty miles to Cnoc dhìreach in eleven days rather than three, as every hearth on the road asks to carry him some part of the way. Calum Beag walks the whole distance at the litter's head, the only bearer who never once hands off his own share of the weight.

title: Tuam Cnoc dhìreach hallowed
summary: Fionnlagh Dall is laid in the ancient, unclaimed burying-ground near Cnoc dhìreach, the first burial there any living hand has set down by name. The Keepers hallow the ground that same season, and it passes from belonging to no one to belonging, by the Hall's own reckoning, to everyone.

title: The grave-keepers of Cnoc dhìreach paid in coal
summary: A handful of families settle by Tuam Cnoc dhìreach to tend the grave, and the Hall pays them one measured handful of coal each a season, the only service the Small-Burning Law is ever known to reward in coal rather than coin or kind.

title: Mòr nic Dhùghaill dies at her own hearth
summary: Found sitting upright in her fireside chair one morning by her own daughter, Mòr nic Dhùghaill dies at sixty-two, two years after Fionnlagh Dall. Her daughter and a niece take up the pot the same week, and the house does not miss a single night's fire.

title: Calum Beag sets a marker at the grave
summary: Calum Beag, now an old man, carries a plain stone the whole way to Cnoc dhìreach on his own back and sets it at Fionnlagh Dall's grave-head with his own hands, cut with nothing but the shape of the stone cup and no name, judging the shape said enough on its own.
